title: TA9-05263
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision in the claims of XXXXXXXXXX (the principal claimant), XXXXX XXXXXXXX (the minor claimant), and XXXXXXXXXX who claim to be citizens of Trinidad and Tobago (Trinidad) and are claiming refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1)(b)1 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).2
The principal claimant was designated representative for the minor claimant.
I have considered counsel's post-hearing written submissions.3 IDENTITY
I am satisfied that the claimants are citizens of Trinidad and as to their personal identities based on certified true copies of their passports.4 ALLEGATIONS
The details of the claimants' allegations appear in the narrative to the principal claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF)5 and were further elaborated upon orally during the hearing.

In short, the claimants are Indo-Trinidadians from a preponderantly Indo-Trinidadian community in XXXXXXX. They allege that they fear for their lives at the hands of an Afro-Trinidadian criminal gang. The principal claimant is a former XXXXXXXXX of some wealth whose business was robbed by the gang. There was also a kidnapping incident involving the minor claimant. In the course of this history of a number of incidents over several years, the gang assaulted and threatened the lives of the claimants.
For the following reasons, I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees and not persons in need of protection.

Crime victim situations with some opposite race elements do not produce a nexus to the race ground under the Convention refugee definition, unless it is clearly shown that the agent of persecution is committing the crimes for race reasons and not for general criminal reasons, such as financial gain.6 While there are race elements to the story here, it is clear from the principal claimant's narrative and testimony that the gang committed the crimes against the claimants for financial gain, which is a general criminal reason.7 I therefore find that the claimant's fear of the criminal gang is not related to a Convention ground and that it has no nexus to the Convention refugee definition.

As to IRPA subsection 97(1)(b) protection, while I acknowledge that the claimants are personally targeted by the gang, I still find, considering this matter within the entire context of the country documents, that the basic genesis and nature of the risk to the claimants from the criminal gang is one that nevertheless arose out of, and therefore is, a type of generalized risk: generalized criminal violence in Trinidad. Refugee Protection Division (RPD) and claimant documents in this claim clearly indicate that drugs, gangs, crime, and criminal violence are widespread problems affecting people generally in Trinidad.8

The fact that these claimants have been specifically and personally targeted by the gang is irrelevant to the determination of whether the risk that they face at the hands of the gang is generalized or not. Every generalized crime victim must have a specific, personal story of targeting to tell in terms of whatever specifically criminal happened to them, just as these claimants have in terms of what has happened to them: after all, if that were not true, generalized crime victims would not, in fact, even be victims of crime. Therefore, the fact that these claimants have been specifically and personally targeted by the gang is indeed irrelevant to the determination of whether the risk that they face at the hands of the gang is generalized within the meaning of subsection 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA or not. The fact that does matter is whether the prospective risk that they face at the hands of the gang is a type of risk that is also faced by a generality of others in Trinidad, or not. Based on the documentary evidence mentioned above clearly indicating that criminal gang activity is a widespread problem in Trinidad, I find the risk that they face at the hands of the gang is a type of risk that is faced by a generality of others in Trinidad and, therefore, that it is a generalized risk that is specifically excepted from protection by subsection 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA.

As with nexus to the Convention refugee definition, some opposite race elements within otherwise generalized crime victim situations do not displace the generalized risk exception in subsection 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA, unless it is clearly shown that the agent of harm is committing the crimes for race reasons and not for general criminal reasons, such as financial gain.9 While there are race elements to the story here, it is clear from the principal claimant's narrative that the gang committed the crimes against the claimants for financial gain, which is a general criminal reason.10 I therefore find that the race elements in this case do not operate to displace the application of the subsection 97(1)(b)(ii) exception.

For the foregoing reasons, I conclude that the claimants are not Convention refugees under section 96 of the IRPA and not persons in need of protection under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. Furthermore, having sufficiently considered the facts, the country evidence and the law in a manner consistent with the context and mission of the RPD, I find that these conclusions fall within the range of reasonable outcomes.11 (signed) "Joel Bousfield" Joel Bousfield November 3, 2011 Date 1 The provisions of subsection 97(1)(b) of the IRPA, which is alternatively relied upon by the claimants for protection in addition to section 96, are reproduced in complete text by counsel and addressed in paragraphs 31-38 of his written submissions dated October 31, 2011. 2 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27. 3 Counsel's written submissions dated October 31, 2011. 4 Exhibit R/A-2. 5 Exhibit C-1. 6 M.C.I. v.
